problem_statement: The paper frames feature selection as a way to reduce high-dimensional classification data while preserving useful information and improving classifier efficiency and performance. It focuses on selecting a subset of features that has high relevance and low redundancy.
problem_statement_quotes: In classification tasks, this overwhelming deluge of data often contains redundant information, which hampers classifier efficiency and performance.

Some methods, such as Maximum Relevance-Minimum Redundancy (MRMR) Algorithm [7], aim to identify the subset of features that exhibit the highest level of information and relevance in a given dataset [8].

The primary aim in searching for an optimal feature subset is to identify a set of features capable of effectively enhancing the classification accuracy in the analysis of the original, high-dimensional dataset.
classical_baseline: The paper treats classical feature selection methods, especially MRMR, as the baseline. It compares its QAOA-based MRMR approach against classical MRMR for selecting feature subsets in classification tasks.
classical_baseline_quotes: Existing classical feature selection algorithms often encounter challenges, such as high computational complexity and vulnerability to local optima.

Some methods, such as Maximum Relevance-Minimum Redundancy (MRMR) Algorithm [7], aim to identify the subset of features that exhibit the highest level of information and relevance in a given dataset [8].

We perform simulated experiments with two goals:

classical_difficulty: The paper says classical feature selection is limited by computational power and storage complexity, and that MRMR can get trapped in local optima. It also states that searching for the global optimum by traversal would likely require exponential time.
classical_difficulty_quotes: Existing classical feature selection algorithms often encounter challenges, such as high computational complexity and vulnerability to local optima.
These approaches are valuable but constrained by computational power and storage complexity.
The defect of this algorithm is obvious: it is a non-global optimal solution algorithm.
If the traversal algorithm of the global optimal solution were used, the time complexity required by the algorithm is probably exponential.
extraction_notes: Motivation is explicit but algorithmic; finance appears only as one benchmark domain, not as a finance-specific problem framing.
